documents.title: Pilot Program: HMC AI-Use Course Policies (DRAFT)
tiers: Level 0: No AI Use Allowed as it Inhibits Learning
documents.summary: A draft, optional syllabus framework from an HMC faculty pilot offering four levels of permitted AI use, from none to open, with example syllabus wording and four constants (Honor Code, acknowledgement, verification, ethics). Instructors choose the level per course or assignment.
documents.stance_why: The document says 'Faculty are not obligated to use these policies' and offers 'four different suggested levels of allowed AI usage'; it sets no stance of its own and hands the choice to instructors, so stance is delegates with tiers listed.

units.why: States the purpose and framework of the pilot: a shared language for allowed AI usages across HMC courses. It is an institution-level framework preamble (P56), not a course rule.
units.anchor: increase clarity for students about what AI usages are allowed or disallowed in our courses

units.why: Says each instructor decides whether to adopt or modify the levels ('not obligated'), so the rule is set per instructor (P04), not by a college-wide mandate.
units.anchor: Faculty are not obligated to use these policies and can modify them

units.why: The document is labelled 'pilot' and invites faculty feedback, so it is provisional and open to revision (P54).
units.anchor: Faculty can share feedback and suggestions by emailing Kathy Van Heuvelen
units.policy: Faculty can share feedback and suggestions on the pilot syllabus language by email or a Google form.

units.why: Defines the scope of the framework as usages rather than named tools, which sets what the policy covers (P61).
units.anchor: the document focuses on usages, as opposed to specific tools

units.why: Defines named levels of AI use (Level 0 to 3), the tier structure (P05).
units.anchor: four different suggested levels of allowed AI usage
units.policy: The document offers four suggested levels of allowed AI usage, ranging from most to least permissive: No AI Use, Time Saving Usage Only, Augmentative Usage Only, Open Use.

units.why: Lets instructors choose the level per course or per assignment, which is per-assignment rule setting (P04); the tiers themselves are coded in the unit above.
units.anchor: whether these policies apply to all student work for your course, or to individual assignments

units.why: Tells instructors to pick the level fitting each class, 'if any', leaving the decision to them (P04).
units.anchor: Consider which, if any, of the policies below are most appropriate for each of your

units.why: Provides template syllabus wording for instructors, supporting stating AI expectations in the syllabus (P09). It is a suggestion, so modality is informs.
units.anchor: Some suggested syllabus language is shown in the boxes below.
units.policy: Suggested syllabus language is provided for instructors to use.

units.why: Asks instructors with a differing policy to relabel it so the numbered levels keep one meaning; the point is clear communication of expectations (P09 over P05, since it is about syllabus labelling, not defining tiers).
units.anchor: please use a different label (other than AI Use Level 0, 1, 2, or 3)
units.policy: Instructors with their own AI usage policy that has different guiding principles should use a label other than AI Use Level 0, 1, 2, or 3.

units.why: Introduces four college-wide constants that apply in every course regardless of level, a shared baseline framework (P56); the constants are coded separately.
units.anchor: Four things remain constant no matter what HMC course you are in

units.why: Students are 'expected to adhere' to the course AI policy, a student duty to comply; it fits students owning compliance (P29) better than a type about the rule's source.
units.anchor: All students in this course are expected to adhere to this course policy
units.policy: All students in this course are expected to adhere to this course policy around generative AI tools.

units.why: Says the Honor Code applies to AI use, so improper AI use is handled as an integrity matter (P36).
units.anchor: HMC students are responsible for upholding the Honor Code, which applies to appropriate use of

units.why: States uncertainty is no excuse for a violation, an enforcement principle that unauthorized use is misconduct even if unintended (P36).
units.anchor: Being unsure about something doesn't excuse a violation of the Honor Code

units.why: Directly tells unsure students to ask the instructor before using AI, matching P10.
units.anchor: ask your instructor for clarification first
units.policy: If you are unclear about whether a specific usage of a generative AI tool is allowed, ask your instructor for clarification first.

units.why: Asks students to report accidental AI use; it works as a self-report provision (P38), though no reduced consequence is stated, so P38 is the nearest fit.
units.anchor: Inadvertent use should also be reported.

units.why: Defines unacknowledged use of sources as plagiarism, classifying it as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Submitting work as if it were your own without proper acknowledgement of your sources is

units.why: Requires acknowledging AI use in the work, a disclosure rule (P24). The tool name and version detail is a separate unit.
units.anchor: at minimum one should always acknowledge when and how AI tools are used
units.policy: At minimum one should always acknowledge when and how AI tools are used in our work.

units.why: Adds the tool name and version to the acknowledgement, the tool-detail citation rule (P25).
units.anchor: along with the specific version and name of the AI tool
units.policy: The acknowledgement of AI use includes the specific version and name of the AI tool.

units.why: Says the exact prompt and full output may need to be shown, matching P25 (prompt and output); 'may be appropriate' keeps it conditional.
units.anchor: show the exact prompt that you used and the AI's full, unedited response
units.policy: In some instances, it may be appropriate to show the exact prompt that you used and the AI's full, unedited response.

units.why: Warns that AI is unreliable and tells students to verify, which is P31.
units.anchor: Generative AI tools aren't reliable sources of information so you should find ways to verify

units.why: Asks students to weigh ethical and environmental impacts, which is P53.
units.anchor: Consider the ethical and environmental impacts of using generative AI tools.

units.why: Prompts students to check permission before uploading material into AI; P49 fits better than P50 because the issue is permission to upload, not data protection.
units.anchor: Before uploading something to a generative AI tool, do you have permission to do so?
units.policy: Before uploading something to a generative AI tool, students should consider whether they have permission to do so.

units.why: Nudges students to question whether AI is the right tool, a mild discouragement without a ban (P03).
units.anchor: consider whether generative AI tools might really be the most appropriate tool

units.why: Advice to instructors to reduce the incentive to use AI by normalizing struggle and offering help; it redesigns course support around AI (P35).
units.anchor: Normalize struggle while learning and provide as many options as possible
units.policy: Instructors should normalize struggle while learning and provide as many options as possible for students to get help.

units.why: Recommends grading changes (partial credit) to lessen incentives for unauthorized AI use, a grading redesign (P35).
units.anchor: avoid all-or-nothing grading in favor of assigning partial credit
units.policy: If possible, instructors should avoid all-or-nothing grading in favor of assigning partial credit for incomplete answers or attempts.

units.why: Tells instructors to restate the AI policy during the term, a communication practice; P09 is the closest communicating-expectations type.
units.anchor: Periodically remind students about the policy
units.policy: Instructors should periodically remind students about the policy, not just on the first day of class.

units.why: Instructors should tell students how and why they use AI themselves, matching P47.
units.anchor: Be transparent about the ways that you use generative AI tools
units.policy: Instructors should be transparent about the ways they use generative AI tools (or not), under what circumstances, and why.

units.why: Advises instructors to point students to reliable alternatives to unreliable AI tools. P31 is addressed to students verifying output, so this instructor practice fits no type and is UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: tell students what tools/resources are reliable sources of information
units.policy: It is helpful for instructors to tell students what tools and resources are reliable sources of information, to give alternatives to unreliable tools.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors recommend reliable sources and alternatives to students as a way to reduce reliance on unreliable AI tools.

units.why: Level 0 rationale: no AI so students build their own understanding, i.e. AI would shortcut skill-building practice (P41).
units.anchor: encourage students to develop their own understanding of and fluency with course material

units.why: Level 0 bans all generative AI in the course, the default prohibition (P01).
units.anchor: the use of any generative AI tools is not allowed in this course
units.policy: The use of any generative AI tools is not allowed in this course.

units.why: Level 0 classes banned AI use as an Honor Code violation, which is P36 (misconduct classification) rather than P01, the ban itself.
units.anchor: will be considered a violation of the HMC Honor Code
units.policy: Use of generative AI tools in a Level 0 course is considered a violation of the HMC Honor Code.

units.why: Lists disallowed Level 0 uses including generating code and images; the core is having AI produce submitted content (P19). Brainstorming, summarizing and checking are folded into the same list by the source.
units.anchor: generate code snippets, images, or videos, revise your writing, or check your work
units.policy: Disallowed uses include, but are not limited to, using generative AI tools to brainstorm ideas, find source materials, summarize ideas, generate code snippets, images, or videos, revise your writing, or check your work.

units.why: Carves out spelling and grammar flagging in the no-AI level while excluding sentence-revision tools; it is a prose-tool rule (P18).
units.anchor: Tools that automatically flag spelling and grammatical errors as you write are allowed
units.policy: Tools that automatically flag spelling and grammatical errors as you write are allowed, but not tools that offer suggested revisions of your sentences.

units.why: Directs multilingual students to ask the instructor about translation tools; P10 chosen over P51 because the action required is to ask first.
units.anchor: If English is not your first language, please ask me about whether tools for translating
units.policy: If English is not your first language, students should ask the instructor whether tools for translating words or texts between languages are allowed.

units.why: Level 1 rationale: AI may save time on mastered or peripheral tasks without supplanting learning, which explains the limit (P41).
units.anchor: save time by outsourcing tasks that you already know how to do well

units.why: Level 1 allows AI-written code for ancillary tasks in a language the student already knows, an explicit conditioned permission for generated code (P16).
units.anchor: writing code to automate an ancillary task for an assignment
units.policy: Level 1 allows writing code to automate an ancillary task for an assignment, where the code is in a language that you are or were once fluent in.

units.why: Level 1 allows AI to check bibliography formatting, a writing-related use (P18).
units.anchor: checking whether your bibliography is consistently formatted

units.why: Level 1 allows AI to do a calculation the student already knows how to do. No type covers calculation help, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: performing a calculation (e.g. an ugly integral) that you already know how to perform
units.uncovered_note: Allowing AI to perform routine calculations the student already knows how to do (time-saving use).

units.why: Level 1 allows AI spelling and grammar checks on writing, a prose rule (P18).
units.anchor: checking your writing for spelling or grammatical errors.

units.why: Analogizes Level 1 AI to a calculator or Wolfram-Alpha. P45 (AI like a collaborator or outside source) is the nearest analogy type, though the analogy here is to a tool.
units.anchor: AI use in this class is comparable to using a graphing calculator or Wolfram-Alpha

units.why: Warns the calculator analogy has limits because AI outputs vary and are opaque, which concerns reliability of output (P31).
units.anchor: AI is not analogous to a calculator
units.policy: AI is not analogous to a calculator: different AI tools may give different responses to the same prompt using methods that are often opaque to the average user.

units.why: Level 1 lists chatbot Q&A on concepts among purposes where AI is 'not permitted'. Subject-matched to P12 (AI as tutor) but with a prohibit stance; no prohibition-of-tutoring type exists.
units.anchor: chatting with an AI chatbot to get answers to conceptual questions about course content;
units.policy: Level 1 does not permit chatting with an AI chatbot to get answers to conceptual questions about course content.

units.why: Level 1 lists brainstorming for a research paper as not permitted; subject-matched to P15 with a prohibit stance.
units.anchor: brainstorming ideas for a research paper;
units.policy: Level 1 does not permit brainstorming ideas for a research paper.

units.why: Level 1 lists AI for major revisions of a paper as not permitted, a prose-specific rule (P18).
units.anchor: major revisions for a paper
units.policy: Level 1 does not permit generative AI for major revisions for a paper.

units.why: Invites students to ask the instructor when unsure about a specific use (P10).
units.anchor: Please ask me if you have any questions about whether a specific usage is allowed

units.why: Points students to human help in place of AI; the closest type is P51 (alternatives are provided), chosen over P41 because the content is a help referral.
units.anchor: please reach out to me, the AE tutors, and/or the Academic Deans
units.policy: Students who want to learn strategies for using study time well should reach out to the instructor, the AE tutors, and/or the Academic Deans.

units.why: Warns that AI outputs are unreliable and must be handled carefully (P31).
units.anchor: AI tools aren't reliable sources of information, so you will need to be careful

units.why: Cautions that permitted use is not always appropriate use, a mild discouragement (P03).
units.anchor: just because you are permitted to use AI doesn't mean it is the best tool

units.why: Level 2 permits AI in learning while students keep intellectual ownership and primary effort; coded P02 as the permissive default stance of the level, with the ownership condition in the next unit.
units.anchor: allow students to use generative AI tools in their learning while retaining intellectual ownership
units.policy: Level 2 allows students to use generative AI tools in their learning while retaining intellectual ownership and primary effort of their work.

units.why: Allows polishing but requires the main ideas and form to be the student's own effort, i.e. students stay the primary problem-solver (P32).
units.anchor: the main ideas and form of your work needs to be the result of your
units.policy: You are allowed to use generative AI tools to enhance or polish your work, but the main ideas and form of your work needs to be the result of your own effort.

units.why: Level 2 allows brainstorming alternatives for the student's own idea (P15).
units.anchor: brainstorming alternatives or options for an idea that you've developed yourself;

units.why: Level 2 allows AI to explain course content, tutor-style use (P12).
units.anchor: seeking alternative explanations for course content to help you understand the material;

units.why: Level 2 allows AI for calculation or ancillary tasks that are not central. No type covers calculation help, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: performing a calculation or ancillary task, but not one that is novel and central
units.uncovered_note: Allowing AI to perform calculations or ancillary tasks that are not novel and central to the student's idea.

units.why: Level 2 allows AI revision of prose for clarity but not for ideas (P18).
units.anchor: revising writing to improve clarity, grammar, or style but not to alter your own ideas;

units.why: Level 2 allows chatbot Q&A on concepts, the tutor use (P12). The phrase repeats Level 1 where it is prohibited, so this is a distinct policy.
units.anchor: chatting with an AI chatbot to get answers to conceptual questions about course content;
units.policy: Level 2 allows chatting with an AI chatbot to get answers to conceptual questions about course content.

units.why: Level 2 allows AI to make practice quizzes (P14).
units.anchor: generating a quiz or practice problems to help you prepare for an exam;

units.why: Level 2 allows AI help finding errors if the student fixes them, matching error help (P13).
units.anchor: getting help to identify a minor error or misunderstanding
units.policy: Level 2 allows checking your work for errors or getting help to identify a minor error or misunderstanding, so that you can fix those errors on your own.

units.why: Level 2 lists AI-generated text, code or media in submitted work as not permitted, P19.
units.anchor: generating text, code, images, videos, or other media that are used, in whole or in
units.policy: Level 2 does not permit generating text, code, images, videos, or other media that are used, in whole or in part, in your submitted work.

units.why: Level 2 forbids help that costs the student primary intellectual ownership, i.e. students own what they submit (P29).
units.anchor: no longer can claim primary intellectual ownership of the work;
units.policy: Level 2 does not permit obtaining help to complete assignments in a manner where you no longer can claim primary intellectual ownership of the work.

units.why: Level 2 lists AI summarizing of sources as not permitted, in contrast with Level 3; summarizing is a study-aid use (P14) with a prohibit stance.
units.anchor: paraphrasing or summarizing sources or complex topics to aid in your understanding.
units.policy: Level 2 does not permit paraphrasing or summarizing sources or complex topics to aid in your understanding.

units.why: Leaves boundary judgment to students, who must gauge how much of their own effort is preserved, i.e. staying the primary thinker (P32).
units.anchor: all require some judgment on your part to determine how much of your own intellectual

units.why: Level 3 openly permits generative AI use, the permissive default (P02).
units.anchor: openly allow students to use generative AI tools in their learning

units.why: Level 3 lists brainstorming as allowed, which is P15.
units.anchor: brainstorming and developing ideas that might form the seed

units.why: Level 3 allows AI-generated text and code in final submissions (P16); the credit condition is a separate unit.
units.anchor: generating text, code, images, videos, and other media that can be used
units.policy: Level 3 allows generating text, code, images, videos, and other media that can be used, in whole or in part, in the final submission.

units.why: Level 3 allows AI summaries of sources, a study-aid use (P14).
units.anchor: summarizing research sources or complex topics to aid in understanding;

units.why: Level 3 allows AI revision of writing (P18).
units.anchor: revising writing to improve clarity, grammar, or style;

units.why: Level 3 allows AI help locating errors (P13).
units.anchor: getting help to locate the source of an error or misunderstanding;

units.why: Level 3 allows AI translation, a language tool rule (P18).
units.anchor: translating text from one language to another.

units.why: Level 3 credits AI like a collaborating lab partner when it plays a significant role, a disclosure rule (P24); the lab-partner analogy is P45 but the required action is crediting, so P24.
units.anchor: they should be credited in the same way that you would share authorship
units.policy: If generative AI tools play a significant role in the genesis of your work, they should be credited in the same way that you would share authorship with a collaborating lab partner in a publication.

units.why: Example syllabus text uses a gym analogy to say that outsourcing practice defeats learning (P41).
units.anchor: Using a forklift to lift weights for you at the gym is pointless and self-defeating

units.why: The upper-division math example sets Level 1 as the course default, so AI is allowed only for narrow listed uses (P05, naming the level; unit stance restrict).
units.anchor: generative AI tools are allowed for Time Saving Usages Only (AI Usage Level 1)
units.policy: Generative AI tools are allowed for Time Saving Usages Only (AI Usage Level 1), with the exception of exams.

units.why: Tells students that policies differ across instructors and to confirm before using AI, which signals one course's policy does not carry over (P11).
units.anchor: it is important to seek clarification from your instructor about what is allowed
units.policy: You may see HMC instructors using other policies, ranging from Level 0 to Level 3; it is important to seek clarification from your instructor about what is allowed before using any generative AI tool.

units.why: Example bans AI on exams for any purpose, P22.
units.anchor: For exams in this course, no generative AI tools are allowed for any purpose

units.why: The Level 0 writing-course example bans AI at every step of the writing process; it is a prose-specific rule (P18) with a prohibit stance.
units.anchor: reading texts, annotating, brainstorming ideas, summarizing, composing, translating, revising sentences, editing, or drafting
units.policy: Disallowed AI uses include, but are not limited to, all steps in the writing process: reading texts, annotating, brainstorming ideas, summarizing, composing, translating, revising sentences, editing, or drafting your writing.

units.why: The writing-course example names Grammarly as covered by the ban, bringing writing-assist tools under a prohibition; P18 (prose tools) fits better than P07, which covers editors and IDEs.
units.anchor: (ChatGPT, Gemini, Grammarly, etc.) is not allowed in this course
units.policy: The use of any generative AI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, Grammarly, etc.) is not allowed in this course.

units.why: Offers multilingual learners a route to ask about translation or grammar software, an access accommodation (P51).
units.anchor: multilingual learner and you believe you have a genuine need for translation or grammar software
units.policy: Multilingual learners who believe they have a genuine need for translation or grammar software should ask the instructor or HMC's multilingual specialist for guidance.

units.why: Writing-course rationale: doing the writing yourself builds skill (P41).
units.anchor: rather than outsourcing tasks to an AI, you will grow as a writer and thinker

documents.title: AI and Students
documents.summary: A short CIS web page telling students to check their instructor's and course's AI policy before using AI, and to prefer the college-licensed tools (Gemini, NotebookLM, Copilot) for data protection. It also asks for mindfulness about copyright and the Honor Code.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'Students must consult with the instructor and course policies' and that its guidelines 'complement-not replace' instructors' instructions; it sets no AI rule of its own, so decisions rest with instructors (delegates).

units.why: Tells students to learn the AI rules for each class and project such as Clinic and thesis, so each context has its own rule (P11); it is not an ask-the-instructor instruction (P10), which is the next unit.
units.anchor: Students should make sure they understand AI guidelines for their classes and other academic projects
units.policy: Students should make sure they understand AI guidelines for their classes and other academic projects (e.g. Clinic, thesis).

units.why: Requires students to consult the instructor and course policy, seeking clarification, before using AI; this is the ask-before-using rule (P10) with a must modality.
units.anchor: Students must consult with the instructor and course policies
units.policy: Students must consult with the instructor and course policies, seeking clarification as needed, before using AI for academic work.

units.why: States that the CIS guidelines do not override faculty instructions, handing decisions to individual instructors (P04).
units.anchor: complement—not replace—the specific instructions and expectations set by individual faculty members

units.why: Directs students to learn which AI Use level applies to a class when faculty use the suggested language; the instruction is to know the class's rule (P11), not to define tiers (P05).
units.anchor: students should make sure they are familiar with which AI Use policy is in place
units.policy: Students should make sure they are familiar with which AI Use policy is in place for the class in question.

units.why: Notes that some faculty use the suggested AI-use-level language, acknowledging the tier framework (P05).
units.anchor: Some HMC faculty are making use of
units.policy: Some HMC faculty make use of suggested language for AI use in courses.

units.why: Says the college provides data-protected AI (Gemini, NotebookLM, Copilot), i.e. sanctioned college tools (P17).
units.anchor: students have access to AI that meets college data protection requirements

units.why: Strongly encourages college-provided tools over consumer ones, a vetted-tool preference for data protection (P50) rather than simply providing tools (P17).
units.anchor: strongly encouraged to use these tools as opposed to consumer versions
units.policy: If a student is using AI for an approved use, they are strongly encouraged to use the college-provided tools as opposed to consumer versions, especially if working with college data.

units.why: Explains the privacy and no-training benefit of college-purchased tools, a data protection rationale (P50).
units.anchor: ensures that your data is private and is not used to train large language models

units.why: Gives a cybersecurity and data-leakage rationale for using college tools (P50).
units.anchor: improves cybersecurity, especially with respect to data leakage

units.why: Asks students working with college data to know the data classification that determines allowed AI tools, protecting confidential data (P50).
units.anchor: understand how the college classifies data and how that affects which AI tools can be
units.policy: If you are working with college data, it is really important to understand how the college classifies data and how that affects which AI tools can be used.

units.why: Warns students to have permission to use others' content such as course materials or another student's work; the content-use concern fits P49, with copyright (P52) secondary.
units.anchor: whether you have permission to use other people's content
units.policy: Students should be mindful of copyright and whether they have permission to use other people's content (e.g. course materials or another student's work).

units.why: Reminds students that Honor Code obligations apply to AI use, a misconduct framework (P36).
units.anchor: Please keep your obligations under the honor code in mind.

notes: Coder B. Course layer deferred in collect file. Pilot document is a template with embedded example syllabi (math, writing) coded as part of the same document. UNCOVERED units: calculation/ancillary-task permission (x2) and instructor advice to recommend reliable alternatives.
